A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Helmsman system and AgentFL-Bench study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison. The original appendix content is retained after renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 16 FL tasks, additional continual-learning comparisons, and evaluation-attempt and human-intervention results.

after.justification: v2 reports original FL benchmark results and adds code-generation comparisons, component ablations, generation-stability results, and input-schema case studies.

M1.justification: The planning, supervised modular coding, and sandboxed evaluation/refinement procedure remains unchanged, including the detailed agent prompts. Additional LLM backbones and component-removal experiments are evaluation configurations rather than revisions to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: The original 16 tasks and their underlying datasets are retained. Appendix A.3 adds limited coverage of different input conditions by testing paraphrased, incomplete, and out-of-schema versions of the Q1 research query.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated code-generation competitors: Codex with GPT-5.1-Codex and Claude Code with Claude-Sonnet-4.5 across all 16 tasks (Tables 7–11). Table 6 also introduces single-agent ReAct comparators. These substantially extend v1's comparisons against FL strategies.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include six configurations on seven queries, additional Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.1 backbones, and generation success, API cost, token consumption, and walltime measurements. Section 4.2 also states 10 cross-device clients, conflicting with the retained 15-client specification in Table 17; an actual change in client count cannot be established.

E4.justification: v2 adds component and HITL ablations (Table 6), backbone comparisons, a Q1 code-structure stability comparison (Appendix A.2), and input-schema robustness cases (Appendix A.3). It removes v1's Figure 4 analysis of evaluation attempts and human intervention. The extended continual-learning comparison in Table 5 is retained.

E5.justification: Tables 2–4 change from point estimates to means with standard deviations over three independent runs, substantially expanding uncertainty reporting for the central benchmark. Appendix A.2 also specifies three independent generation runs. v1 already averaged its evaluation-attempt figure over three runs; the PDFs do not establish an increase in the earlier benchmark's run count.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 replace the reported values: for example, Helmsman's Q1 accuracy changes from 76.26 to 76.71 ± 0.43 and Q16 from 51.04 to 50.95 ± 1.09. Table 5 is unchanged. New Table 11 reports 100% success for Helmsman with Sonnet-4.5 or GPT-5.1, versus 37.5% for Codex and 43.75% for Claude Code. These additions and the removal of v1's intervention results do not establish a same-setting improvement in autonomy.

T1.justification: The simulation, diagnosis, code-correction equations, and termination reasoning in Section 3 are unchanged. The added appendices contain empirical evaluations and explanations, without new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: end-to-end agentic FL synthesis, the 16-task AgentFL-Bench, and competitiveness with handcrafted FL baselines. The additional experiments do not redefine these stated contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the explicit computational-cost and 62.5%-automation limitation discussion with a claim of 100% full automation and presents human expertise as optional assistance. New interpretations attribute success to system components and coordination, and treat consistent folder structures as evidence of reproducibility. The general non-convergence caveat in Section 3.3 remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds concrete API-cost, token-use, and walltime disclosures for the generation experiments and identifies additional backbone configurations. The extensive implementation prompts remain unchanged. The 80/20 split now mentioned in the main text was already specified, with seed 42, in v1's task-coder appendix.

R1.justification: The related-work section and reference list are unchanged. Appendix A.1 adds focused positioning against Codex and Claude Code, arguing advantages in generation effectiveness and cost efficiency beyond the earlier emphasis on handcrafted FL strategies.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Multi-Agent Collaboration' to 'Collaborative LLM Agents,' and the implementation and discussion passages receive localized revisions. Three new appendix sections precede the renumbered original appendices; most existing prose and document organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables, a code-structure comparison figure, and four dialogue figures. The original evaluation-attempt Figure 4 is removed, while the new Figure 4 presents different content. Tables 2–4 gain uncertainty formatting, Table 3 moves to page 7, and Figure 2 is reduced in size.

improvement.justification: The agent-level comparisons and component ablations address an important gap in v1: FL accuracy comparisons alone did not establish the value of the proposed agent system against alternative code-generation approaches. Reporting variability across three runs also strengthens the central empirical evidence. These gains substantially improve the paper, although removal of the intervention/cost limitation analysis, stronger autonomy wording, and conflicting client-count specifications weaken transparency.
